title: Units, dimensions and vectors
note: Every physical quantity is a number times a unit. SI builds all units from a few base units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd). A scalar has only size; a vector has size and direction, and you add vectors by adding their components.

read.title: Why units and vectors come first
text: A number in physics means nothing until it has a unit. Saying a car travels "30" could mean 30 meters per second or 30 miles per hour, and those differ by more than a factor of two. The SI system avoids confusion by building every unit from a handful of base units. A newton is a kg·m/s², a joule is a newton times a meter, and a watt is a joule per second. Prefixes such as milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), and mega (10⁶) scale those units up or down by powers of ten.

Units also give a free check. In a correct equation every term has the same dimensions, so you can never add a length to a time. If an answer for a speed comes out in kilograms, something went wrong. Dimensional analysis cannot catch a missing pure number such as ½, though.

Many quantities need a direction as well as a size. Displacement, velocity, force, and momentum are vectors; mass, time, energy, and temperature are scalars. To add vectors, break each one into components, add the x parts and the y parts separately, then rebuild the result with the Pythagorean theorem and an inverse tangent. Walking 3 m east and 4 m north leaves you 5 m from where you started, not 7 m.
